title: The Twelve Tables
objective: After this level you can explain why Rome wrote down its laws and what that changed.
summary: Around 450 BCE Rome wrote its laws on the Twelve Tables in the Forum, so patrician judges could no longer bend unwritten custom.

cards.headline: A law you can’t read is a law someone else controls.
Law in public
cards.body: Around 450 BCE, Rome wrote down its laws on the Twelve Tables and displayed them in the Forum. Plebeians had demanded it: until then, patrician judges could interpret unwritten custom as they pleased. Now anyone could check the rules, at least in principle.

cards.headline: Everyday rules
cards.body: The Twelve Tables covered ordinary life: debt, property, family and damage to others. They became the foundation of Roman law. Centuries later, Cicero remembered learning them by heart as a schoolboy, though he said boys no longer did.

cards.context: They were probably destroyed when the Gauls sacked Rome. The laws survive only in quotations by later writers.

cards.headline: Written law: established
learned: The Twelve Tables were written around 450 BCE

questions.explanation: The Twelve Tables were Rome’s first written law code, displayed in the Forum around 450 BCE.

questions.prompt: Why did plebeians want the laws written down?

options.label: So they could vote on each law again
So patrician judges couldn’t bend unwritten custom
So the laws could be sent to other cities
options.rationale: The point was fairness at home.

options.label: So priests could read them aloud

questions.explanation: Written, public laws meant patricians could no longer interpret custom however they liked.

questions.prompt: From Level 14: the Twelve Tables were a win in which struggle?

options.label: The war against the Etruscans
options.rationale: The Tables were an internal reform.

questions.explanation: Written laws were one of the plebeians’ gains in the Conflict of the Orders.
